newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba/Bonn tensions revived by asset revaluation.
newsitem.headline: Buba/Bonn tensions revived by asset revaluation.

text.p: The Bundesbank's stubborn rejection of Bonn's plans to revalue its official reserves has brought to the surface a decades-old debate over who holds the reins of German economic policy.

Through its legal mandate to temper inflation and protect the mark, the Bundesbank has periodically fought pitched battles with Bonn on broad economic issues, helping it earn a nickname as the "fourth branch of government."
"In Germany, we have conditions where Bonn and the Bundesbank are sometimes thrown into conflict," said Guenther Thumann, economist at Salomon Brothers in London.

David Marsh, in his book, "The Bundesbank, the Bank that Rules Europe," said that the central bank and Bonn have had serious policy disagreements a dozen times and that three chancellors owe their downfalls directly to the Bundesbank.

At the root of the sometimes uneasy relationship is the Bundesbank Law of 1957 which grants the central bank "independence of government direction," but also binds it to support the federal government in its role as maker of "general economic policy."
Analysts said the law is so vague as to allow for several interpretations and give the Bundesbank room to challenge Bonn when it feels it has a chance of winning.
Ellen Kennedy writes in her book, "The Bundesbank": "This paragraph has been the focus of much political debate and can be interpreted in two opposing ways."

Former Bundesbank chief Karl Otto Poehl, for example, told the Financial Times in 1989 that the Bundesbank was a "form of a state within the state -- an economic policy counterweight to the government."
His successor Helmut Schlesinger however stressed in 1992 that the Bundesbank "was not a government" and supported Bonn's plans for uniting the deutsche mark with the east German currency.

The latest example of this tension surfaced two weeks ago when Finace Minister Theo Waigel flew to Frankfurt to present a plan for revaluing the Bundesbank's official reserves in an effort to raise money for trimming the government's budget shortfall.

Aimed at helping Germany qualify for European monetary union, the Bundesbank has attacked the plan as an invasion of its independence and a threat to the stability of the future European single currency, the euro.
Already there have been rumours in financial markets that the fight would force either Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer or Waigel to resign.
History offers a mixed picture of who prevails in showdowns between the central bank and Bonn.

In 1991, the government and the Bundesbank clashed over at what level to convert the east mark to deutsche mark, a fight that eventally led to Poehl's resignation and the central bank losing out to Bonn's one-for-one conversion plan.

In 1972, however, it was the Bundesbank that emerged victorious when Finance Minister Karl Schiller tried to pressure the Bundesbank into allowing the mark to float freely on currency markets in an attempt to blunt heavy capital inflows in to Germany.

Bundesbank President Karl Klasen, however, favoured imposing capital controls -- a policy accepted by Chancellor Willi Brandt. Schiller was forced to eventually resign because of the public disagreement.

Although government interference in central banking dates back to 1955 when Konrad Adenauer tried to intervene in the Bank deutscher Laender's credit policies, the first real test of wills between the Bundesbank and Bonn took place in 1961.

The central bank then was forced to make an embarassing climb down to Economics Minister Ludwig Erhard who had pressured the bank to revalue the currency, eventually forcing Bundesbank President Karl Blessing to agree to a five percent revaluation of the mark that he had fought for months.

"A look at the history of Bundesbank battles shows the Bundesbank has generally won when it was over interest rates," said Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs. "When it was about fundamental policy issues, the government generally has won."
